Papagelou v AAI Ltd t/as AAMI [2025] NSWPIC 567; 
 (21 October 2025)

system:
You are coding NSW motor accident decisions for a research dataset. Read the decision text supplied and assign each ordinal score from the text alone.

Score each dimension INDEPENDENTLY. A decision describing a severe case will score high on some dimensions and not others: severe physical injury does not by itself imply a contested proceeding, a disputed liability, or a prominent psychological component. Judge each scale against its own definition and resist letting an overall impression of severity carry across the scales.

If the text does not support a judgement on a dimension, give the lowest score rather than guessing upward, and say so in `uncertain`.

DECISION TEXT:
--- Catchwords ---
MOTOR ACCIDENTS - Damages assessment; injuries exceed 10% whole person impairment (WPI); credibility and veracity of claimant; requirement for spinal fusion; psychological injury; post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); Held

– claimant retains significant transferable skills; claimant able to continue in employment with some restrictions; scope for significant further improvement; overpayment by insurer; claimant not accepted in respect of payroll management assertions; claimant credibility; claimant able to pursue business and development opportunities; uncertainty as to calculations of past and future economic loss; requirement for buffer to reflect loss of earnings.

ASSESSMENT CONFERENCE REPORT

--- Key Paragraphs ---
[para 3] Sets scope: non-threshold injuries exceeding 10% WPI, damages heads to assess, and Fox v Wood agreement.
3. The parties have agreed that the claimant's injuries are non-threshold injuries and that his injuries exceed 10% whole person impairment (WPI). Accordingly, the matters requiring assessment are the claimant's economic loss and non-economic loss. The parties have agreed that allowance ought to be made for tax paid on the payments to the claimant (Fox v Wood) of

$53,819.

[para 13] Finds residual work capacity and transferable skills; key to economic loss.
13. As I have outlined above the claimant is troubled significantly by his cervical spinal injury but it does not prevent him from undertaking lighter tasks or working in a sedentary occupation. The report of Professor Bright dated 2 May 2025, suggesting the claimant was both self-limiting and not an entirely reliable historian, does identify a capacity for work and noting the claimant has significant transferable skills derived from many years working in the hospitality industry, mainly in managerial and ownership roles. He noted the report of the claimant's treating psychologist, Nick Cherrie dated 28 September 2023, which states: "It is my understanding that Angelo has shown some improvement with his driving, but he is still experiencing symptoms of anxiety and depression around his physical recovery."

[para 15] Expresses scope for significant improvement; frames reduced awards.
15. The claimant is 55 years old I do not accept that the condition, both physical and psychological, is of such severity as to prevent him from undertaking any gainful type of employment. I do not accept that the medical material is of such nature as to suggest significant improvement is not possible. Indeed in, in my view, the medical material supports the insurer's contention that there is scope for significant further improvement in the claimant's physical and psychological condition. THE CLAIMANT

[para 21] Rejects claimant’s account regarding payroll; credibility finding.
21. I do not accept the claimant's contention that he was unaware that he was being overpaid during this period. I do not accept that he never checked his account to see how much was going into it. I do not accept his answer at the assessment conference indicating that he was not responsible for the preparation of the business activity statement. I do not accept his assertion that he didn't need to know wages. At the assessment conference, the claimant conceded that payslips have been emailed to the insurer and that the claimant knew that he was being paid. This is contrary to his assertion in his statement dated 7 August 2025 in which he stated that he did not receive payslips from work, he stated position that: "The accounting software picked up and paid my pre-agreed superannuation; it needed to reflect the previous wage."

[para 22] Concludes claimant lacks credibility on earnings loss; central to buffers.
22. I accept the insurance submission that the claimant was seeking to avoid any responsibility for the overpayment. I accept the insurance submission The claimant lacks credibility in respect to his assertions of loss of earnings consequence on the motor vehicle accident.

[para 28] Post-accident business and development activities undermine claimed loss.
28. As was outlined at the assessment conference the claimant has invested in property for development following the accident. The cafe which employed the claimant was purchased in 2017 for $390,000 and sold in 2023 for $1.6 million. The claimant has been investing in the land at Sanctuary Point to facilitate its rezoning and allow development by the building of apartments. The claimant agreed that payments had been made for this purpose in August 2023 and March 2024. These business and development opportunities being undertaken by the claimant, since the motor vehicle accident, contradict his assertion in his statement that this is no longer possible. NON-ECONOMIC LOSS

[para 38] Methodology for past economic loss buffer and weekly proxies.
38. As I have outlined above there is considerable uncertainty in respect to the precise loss sustained by the claimant. In this regard I consider it appropriate to provide for a buffer in respect to the claimant's past economic loss loosely based on a calculation of wage loss of in the order of $900 per week from the time of the accident to the time of the sale of the cafe, and thereafter a loss of in the order of $1,200 per week. This is reflective of, for the first period, and an impairment on earning capacity of roughly 50% on his pre-accident capacities and, since the sale of the business, a loss of earnings and earning capacity loosely based on about a two thirds loss of his pre-accident earnings and earning capacity. Whilst the claimant was, essentially, self-employed he was receiving some superannuation payments from the entity which paid his salary. This gives rise to a further loss of employee superannuation contributions which, in my view, would be allowed in the calculation for past economic loss.

[para 42] Basis for future economic loss buffer: pre-injury earnings and weekly net loss.
42. I note the claimant's pre-accident earnings of in excess of $1,800 per week, I consider it appropriate to allow a buffer loosely based on a net loss of earnings of in the order of $1,200 per week. This is a loss reflective of an impaired earning capacity of between 50 and 75%. By making an allowance for the remainder of the claimant's working life, had he not been injured in the subject motor vehicle accident, and factor in for vicissitudes being offset by an allowance for loss of employer superannuation contributions, this gives rise to a figure of, in the order of, $550,000.

[para 45] Final quantification and credits; dispositive outcome.
45. I assess the quantification of this claim in the amount of $1,100,000. I note the insurer is to have credit of $305,472.29.

Assign each score:
  Injury Burden Intensity (0-4): overall physical burden of the injuries: 0 minimal, 4 catastrophic/multiple major injuries
  Treatment Burden (0-3): extent of treatment, surgery and ongoing care: 0 none or minimal, 3 extensive surgery and long-term care
  Work Impact Severity (0-3): loss of working capacity: 0 none, 3 total incapacity
  Legal Procedural Complexity (0-3): procedural complexity of the proceeding: 0 straightforward, 3 heavily contested
  Psychological Injury Emphasis (0-2): weight the decision gives to psychological injury: 0 none, 2 central
  Liability Clarity (0-2): how clear fault is: 0 seriously disputed, 2 clear or admitted
  Causation Complexity (0-2): difficulty attributing the condition to the accident: 0 straightforward, 2 heavily contested
  Pre-existing Condition Salience (0-2): how prominent a prior condition is in the decision: 0 absent, 2 central
